chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdullah, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) prayed with his companions during the Expedition of Dhat al-Riqa', the Prayer of Fear. So he separated his companions into two groups: he stationed one group facing the enemy and one group behind him. He said Takbir, and they said Takbir. He recited, and they listened silently. He bowed (Ruku'), so they bowed. He prostrated (Sajdah), so they prostrated.

Then the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) completed (the prayer) standing, and they prayed one Rak'ah by themselves. Then some of them offered Salam to the others. Then they went out to their companions, so they stood facing the enemy, and their companions came over, so they stood behind the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family). So he prayed one Rak'ah with them. Then he performed Tashahhud and offered Salam upon them. So they stood and prayed one Rak'ah by themselves, then some of them offered Salam to the others.
ai.seo_question: How did the Prophet Muhammad perform the Prayer of Fear (Salat al-Khaf) with his companions during battle?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi provides a detailed procedural account of Salat al-Khaf, highlighting the practical division of troops into two groups to maintain vigilance while performing prayer. It underscores the flexibility of Islamic jurisprudence in adapting ritual acts to military exigencies, a key theme in Shia legal theory regarding the suspension of full ritual completeness during combat. The text emphasizes the sequential nature of the prayer, where each group completes their rak'ahs individually under the Imam's guidance, reflecting the balance between spiritual obligation and physical security.
